Slavery (Biblical Context)
SLAY-vuh-ree
noun (Christian ethics)
The substantive question of how Scripture addresses slavery (Hebrew ebed, Greek doulos). The biblical material includes the regulation (not endorsement) of various ancient bond-service systems, the substantive distinction between Hebrew indentured servitude and chattel slavery, the condemnation of man-stealing, and the gospel principle that undermined ancient slavery from within (Philemon; Galatians 3:28).

📖 Biblical Definition

The substantive question of how Scripture addresses slavery (Hebrew ebed, servant/slave; Greek doulos, servant/slave). The biblical material requires substantive careful reading. (1) The OT regulated rather than endorsed ancient bond-service: the Mosaic law regulated the various forms of ancient servitude (Hebrew indentured servitude to pay debts, with release in the seventh year and at Jubilee, Exodus 21:2-6; Leviticus 25:39-43; the substantive protections for servants, Exodus 21:20-21, 26-27; Deuteronomy 23:15-16, the substantive prohibition of returning an escaped slave). Hebrew servitude was substantively different from later chattel slavery: it was typically temporary (debt-bondage with release), regulated for the protection of the servant, and not based on race or kidnapping. (2) Man-stealing is condemned as a capital crime: the kidnapping and selling of persons (the basis of the transatlantic slave trade) is explicitly condemned (Exodus 21:16, he that stealeth a man, and selleth him... shall surely be put to death; 1 Timothy 1:10, menstealers among the lawless and disobedient). (3) The NT regulated the existing Roman slave system while undermining it from within: the NT addressed the universal Greco-Roman slave system (in which a substantial fraction of the population were slaves) by regulating the master-slave relationship (Ephesians 6:5-9; Colossians 3:22-4:1; 1 Peter 2:18-21) and by introducing the gospel principle that undermined the system from within (Philemon, where Paul sends the converted runaway slave Onesimus back to his master Philemon as a brother beloved; 1 Corinthians 7:21, counsel to gain freedom if possible; Galatians 3:28, the equal standing of slave and free in Christ). The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the slavery question with substantive honesty: Scripture regulated ancient bond-service systems without endorsing them as the ideal; the chattel slavery of the transatlantic trade was founded on man-stealing, which Scripture condemns as a capital crime; the gospel principle of the equal dignity of all image-bearers and the brotherhood of all believers in Christ undermined and ultimately abolished slavery wherever the gospel took deep root (the substantive role of evangelical Christians like William Wilberforce in the abolition movement); the contemporary critical use of biblical slavery material to discredit Scripture misreads the substantive distinction between regulation and endorsement and ignores Scripture's condemnation of man-stealing.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The question of how Scripture addresses slavery; the OT regulated (not endorsed) ancient bond-service with substantive protections; man-stealing is condemned as a capital crime (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10); the NT regulated Roman slavery while undermining it from within (Philemon; Galatians 3:28).

SLAVERY (BIBLICAL CONTEXT), n. (Christian ethics) How Scripture addresses slavery (Hebrew ebed, Greek doulos). (1) OT regulated rather than endorsed ancient bond-service: Hebrew indentured servitude (debt-bondage with seventh-year and Jubilee release, Exodus 21:2-6; Leviticus 25:39-43); substantive protections (Exodus 21:20-27; Deuteronomy 23:15-16, prohibition of returning an escaped slave). (2) Man-stealing condemned as capital crime (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10, menstealers) — the basis of the transatlantic slave trade. (3) NT regulated Roman slavery while undermining it from within (Ephesians 6:5-9; Philemon, Onesimus as a brother beloved; 1 Corinthians 7:21; Galatians 3:28). Evangelical role in abolition (Wilberforce).

📖 Key Scripture

Exodus 21:16 — "And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death."

1 Timothy 1:9-10 — "Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient... for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine."

Philemon 1:15-16 — "For perhaps he therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever; Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?"

Galatians 3:28 — "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The contemporary critical use of biblical slavery material to discredit Scripture misreads the distinction between regulation and endorsement, ignores Scripture's condemnation of man-stealing, and overlooks the gospel principle that undermined and abolished slavery.

expand to see more

The substantive question of biblical slavery requires careful honest reading against two opposing distortions. The first distortion is the contemporary critical use of biblical slavery material to discredit Scripture as a pro-slavery document. This misreads the substantive distinction between regulation and endorsement: Scripture regulated the ancient bond-service systems that universally existed in the ancient world (as it regulated divorce, polygamy, and other realities) without endorsing them as the ideal; the OT Hebrew servitude system was substantively different from later chattel slavery (temporary debt-bondage with release, regulated for the servant's protection, not race-based or kidnapping-based); and crucially, Scripture condemns man-stealing — the kidnapping and selling of persons that was the foundation of the transatlantic slave trade — as a capital crime (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10). The second distortion is the historic pro-slavery misuse of Scripture by antebellum Southern theologians (including R. L. Dabney and others) to defend race-based chattel slavery; this misuse ignored the man-stealing condemnation that rendered the transatlantic trade unbiblical at its foundation and inverted the gospel principle of the equal dignity of all image-bearers. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive honest reading: Scripture regulated ancient bond-service without endorsing it; condemned the man-stealing on which chattel slavery was founded; and introduced the gospel principle (the equal dignity of all image-bearers, the brotherhood of all believers in Christ, Galatians 3:28; Philemon) that undermined and ultimately abolished slavery wherever the gospel took deep root — the substantive role of evangelical Christians like William Wilberforce, the Clapham Sect, and the broader evangelical abolition movement.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

OT regulation of bond-service with protections; man-stealing condemned (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10); NT regulation undermining from within (Philemon; Galatians 3:28); evangelical abolition (Wilberforce).
